unlisted_practices: Regulators should harmonize device and pharmaceutical regulatory pathways for AI tools that function simultaneously as diagnostics, predictors, and treatment-guiding systems.
Regulators should operationalize lifecycle-based evaluation models that integrate real-world evidence, adaptive validation, and continuous performance monitoring into routine oversight.
Regulators should adopt Predetermined Change Control Plans so that permissible AI model modifications, retraining criteria, acceptance thresholds, and post-update verification are defined in advance.

Regulators should separate assurance of the computational platform layer from validation of the analytical pipeline and clinical application layer, while still validating the complete system for its intended use.
Developers should build interpretable glass-box AI systems rather than opaque black-box systems.
Developers and regulators should clarify the intended use of an AI tool (screening, triage, or therapy) so that risk can be mapped to required evidence.
Regulators should use regulatory sandboxes to test novel AI systems under regulatory supervision before full market authorization.
Developers should use federated learning and privacy-preserving analytics to develop and validate AI across distributed datasets without centralizing sensitive data.
Developers and regulators should control and document pre-analytical factors, batch effects, and metadata consistency to ensure data integrity and provenance in multi-omics AI.

Developers and regulators should establish digital evidence ecosystems with standardized repositories for datasets, benchmarks, and performance metrics to support reproducibility and post-market surveillance.

screen.reason: This is a commentary discussing regulatory frameworks, data integrity, algorithm transparency, and validation pathways for AI-enabled multi-omics in precision medicine.
